definition: Of the carbon-based combustion byproducts, carbon dioxide is a normal, nontoxic result of complete combustion whose concern is purely climatic, while carbon monoxide results from incomplete combustion (insufficient oxygen) and is acutely toxic to humans.
core_idea: Carbon dioxide and water are the primary hydrocarbon combustion byproducts and aren't pollutants in the traditional toxicity sense (water isn't a pollutant at all); the real health-hazard byproduct is carbon monoxide, which forms specifically when combustion is oxygen-starved.
key_points: Water and carbon dioxide are the primary byproducts of hydrocarbon combustion; water is not considered a pollutant at all.
Carbon dioxide is colorless, odorless, and nontoxic, and would not be considered a pollutant except for its effect on global climate.
Carbon monoxide is highly toxic precisely because it is highly reactive, and forms when combustion is incomplete due to insufficient oxygen.
relationships: Directly ties back to the major-pollutant-categories item, elaborating the distinction between CO2 and CO first introduced there.
trading_implications: Because CO2 is climate-relevant rather than acutely toxic, its regulatory treatment (aggregate, market-based) differs from CO, NOx, and SOx, which are handled as direct health/air-quality hazards.
caveats: CO2 is often lumped in with 'toxic emissions,' but the source is explicit that it poses no direct health threat — the same byproduct as normal breathing or exercise — unlike carbon monoxide.
